slides.note: Primary retroperitoneal means the organ formed behind the peritoneum and never had a mesentery. The suprarenal gland sits in its own compartment of renal fascia, so a kidney can be removed for transplant, or can drop (nephroptosis), while the gland stays attached to the diaphragm.

Find the left renal vein: it crosses anterior to the aorta, just below the SMA (superior mesenteric artery), to reach the IVC (inferior vena cava). The renal arteries are hidden posterior to the renal veins. Each suprarenal gland sits on the superomedial pole of its kidney. Each ureter runs down on psoas major, and the gonadal (testicular) vessels cross in front of it.

Posterior view, so the patient's left is on your left. The left kidney sits higher because the liver pushes the right one down (by about 2.5 cm). The transpyloric plane (L1) passes through the left hilum (about 5 cm from the midline) and the superior pole of the right kidney. The 12th rib crosses the upper part of each kidney.

Renal fascia is also called Gerota fascia. Its anterior and posterior layers are closed above and medially, but only loosely joined below. So pus or blood around a kidney can track down into the pelvis, but not across to the other kidney, because the fascia blends with the renal vessels at the hilum.

Layers from inside out: fibrous capsule → perirenal (perinephric) fat → renal fascia → pararenal (paranephric) fat → transversalis fascia. Don't confuse them: perirenal fat is inside the fascia, hugging the kidney; pararenal fat is outside it, mostly behind.

Cross-section seen from below, as on a CT scan. Follow the renal fascia (purple line): its anterior and posterior layers wrap the kidney and perinephric fat, and paranephric fat lies outside, behind. The kidney rests on psoas major medially and quadratus lumborum posteriorly, so its hilum faces anteromedially.

Section at L2 seen from below, so the patient's right is on your left. Find the left renal vein passing between the SMA in front and the aorta behind on its way to the IVC; this is where it gets squeezed in nutcracker syndrome. The duodenum and right colic flexure lie directly in front of the right kidney.

(A) The lumbar approach to the kidney: the surgeon enters from the back, between the back muscles and the flat abdominal muscles, then opens the renal fascia and perinephric fat. The subcostal nerve (T12) and the L1 anterior ramus (iliohypogastric and ilio-inguinal nerves) run diagonally across the back of the kidney, so they are at risk here.

Simple rule: the glomeruli and the coiled (convoluted) tubules sit in the cortex. The straight parts (the straight ends of the proximal and distal tubules, the loops of Henle and the medullary collecting ducts) run down into the medulla.

Follow the urine: renal papilla (tip of a pyramid) → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter. Renal columns are cortex dipping down between the pyramids; the interlobar vessels run in them. Fat in the renal sinus surrounds the pelvis and calyces.

A nephron = renal corpuscle (glomerulus inside Bowman's capsule) + tubule: proximal tubule → loop of Henle → distal tubule, which empties into a collecting duct. In (c), the efferent arteriole leaves the glomerulus and forms a second capillary bed around the tubules (peritubular capillaries) before blood returns to the renal vein.

Follow the colors: blue = proximal tubule, white = thin limbs of the loop, orange = distal tubule (thick ascending limb + distal convoluted tubule), gray = collecting duct, which opens on the papilla. Juxtamedullary nephrons (corpuscle next to the medulla) have long loops reaching deep into the inner medulla; cortical nephrons have short loops. The macula densa (black) is where the distal tubule touches its own glomerulus.

Each colored patch is where that structure touches the kidney. On the right kidney the liver covers most of the front, and the duodenum lies over the hilum. Behind, only the 12th rib crosses the right kidney; the higher left kidney is crossed by both the 11th and 12th ribs. Below the ribs the kidney rests on psoas major, quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis, from medial to lateral.

Also called Morison pouch. When a patient lies on the back, it is a low, gravity-dependent spot of the upper abdomen, so free fluid such as blood (hemoperitoneum) pools here early. It is one of the first places checked on bedside trauma ultrasound.

The renal arteries leave the aorta at the L1–L2 disc, just below the SMA. The right one is longer, because the aorta lies left of the midline, and it passes behind the IVC. Segmental arteries are end arteries (no connections between them), so blocking one kills its whole segment, and each segment can be removed surgically on its own.

Correction: the interlobar arteries are missing; they come right before the arcuate arteries. Full order: renal → segmental → (lobar) → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular (cortical radiate) → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries / vasa recta (straight capillaries running beside the loops of Henle).

Find the right renal artery passing posterior to the IVC, and the long left renal vein crossing anterior to the aorta just below the SMA. Each suprarenal gland gets three arteries: superior (from the inferior phrenic artery), middle (from the aorta) and inferior (from the renal artery).

Where each artery runs: interlobar arteries climb between the pyramids (in the renal columns); arcuate arteries arch over the pyramid bases at the cortex–medulla border; cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries run out through the cortex and give off the afferent arterioles. The renal artery splits into anterior and posterior branches before the hilum.

Note the accessory renal artery to the lower pole of the left kidney. Extra renal arteries (about 30% of people) are embryonic vessels that did not regress as the kidney rose. They are end arteries, so tying one off kills that part of the kidney, and a lower-pole artery can cross and obstruct the ureter.

Don't confuse the sides: on the right, the suprarenal and gonadal veins drain straight into the IVC; only on the left do they drain into the renal vein. So a blocked left renal vein (nutcracker, a left kidney tumor growing into the vein) backs blood into the left testicular vein and can cause a left varicocele. Nutcracker syndrome and renal vein entrapment syndrome are the same thing.

Lateral view from the left. The SMA leaves the aorta at a sharp angle. The left renal vein and, just below it, the 3rd part of the duodenum pass through that angle. If the angle narrows, the SMA squeezes the vein against the aorta like a nutcracker.

Correction: in NCS (nutcracker syndrome), nausea and vomiting come from squeezing of the 3rd part of the duodenum in the same SMA–aorta angle, not from splanchnic veins. The rest comes from back-pressure in the left renal vein: swollen veins in the kidney leak blood into the urine (hematuria; over time, anemia). The left gonadal vein drains into the renal vein, so men get left testicular pain and women left lower quadrant (ovarian vein) pain.

Sympathetic fibers come mainly from the least splanchnic nerve (T12), relay in the aorticorenal ganglion and reach the kidney along the renal artery; they constrict the afferent and efferent arterioles. Parasympathetic fibers come from the vagus. Pain fibers run back with the sympathetic fibers to T10–L1, so kidney pain is felt in the flank and low back.

Follow each ureter down. It lies on the psoas major and passes posterior to the testicular (gonadal) vessels. It enters the pelvis by crossing the external iliac artery just past the common iliac bifurcation. Near the bladder, the ductus deferens crosses superior to it; nothing else lies between the ureter and the peritoneum there.

Find where the ureter passes inferior to the uterine artery beside the cervix: "water under the bridge." When a surgeon ties the uterine artery in a hysterectomy (removal of the uterus), the ureter can be clamped or cut here. The ovarian vessels also lie close to the ureter at the pelvic brim, a second injury point.

This drawing uses old names: genitocrural = genitofemoral nerve; external cutaneous = lateral femoral cutaneous nerve; vas deferens = ductus deferens. Note that the middle narrowing is where the ureter passes anterior to (over) the iliac artery.

A pyelogram is an X-ray taken after contrast dye fills the renal pelvis and ureters (here pushed up from the bladder through a catheter). Red 1–3 = the three normal narrowings: (1) ureteropelvic junction, (2) crossing of the external iliac artery at the pelvic brim, (3) passage through the bladder wall. Black arrows = renal papillae bulging into minor calices.

The abdominal ureter gets small branches from the renal (most constant), gonadal (testicular or ovarian), aorta and common iliac arteries. The pelvic ureter gets branches from the internal iliac system (superior and inferior vesical; uterine in females). The ascending and descending twigs join into one thin chain along the ureter wall, so stripping the ureter in surgery can starve it of blood.

Find the "ureteric branch" labels top to bottom: renal → aorta → ovarian and common iliac → inferior vesical → superior vesical. Each supplies the stretch of ureter nearest to it. In the abdomen the branches reach the ureter from its medial side; in the pelvis, from its lateral side.

Find the accessory renal artery on the left: an extra artery from the aorta to the lower pole, left over from the kidney's embryonic ascent. A lower-pole artery can cross anterior to the ureter and block it. At the bottom, branches from the superior vesical arteries climb up to the lower ureter.

Lymph follows the veins. Kidney and upper ureter drain to the lumbar nodes: caval nodes beside the IVC (inferior vena cava) and aortic nodes beside the aorta. Middle ureter → common iliac nodes. Lower (pelvic) ureter → common, external or internal iliac nodes.

Inset: inside the kidney, lymph vessels run beside the arteries (interlobular → arcuate → interlobar) and leave at the hilum (arrows show flow). Main picture: they reach the lateral aortic (lumbar) nodes, then the lumbar trunks carry lymph up to the cisterna chyli (the sac where the thoracic duct begins).

The plexuses are the renal, abdominal aortic and superior hypogastric plexuses. Pain fibers from a stretched ureter run back with the sympathetic nerves to cord segments T11–L2. The brain reads the pain as coming from the skin those segments supply, so it is felt on the same side from the loin to the groin.

The renal plexus (green, around the renal artery) carries both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers into the kidney and down the upper ureter. Its sympathetic input comes mainly from the least splanchnic nerve, which synapses in the aorticorenal ganglion. Its parasympathetic input comes from the vagus (posterior vagal trunk).

Red = sympathetic, blue = parasympathetic, black = pain (afferent) fibers; solid = preganglionic, dashed = postganglionic. Sympathetic fibers leave cord segments T10–L1 in the lesser, least and 1st lumbar splanchnic nerves and synapse in the aorticorenal and renal ganglia. Pain fibers run the same path back (kidney T10–L1; ureter down to L2). Parasympathetic: vagus to the kidney; pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) to the lower ureter.

A staghorn stone fills the renal pelvis and branches into the calices like a deer antler. It is usually made of struvite and forms in infections with urease-making bacteria such as Proteus. Small loose stones in the pelvis are the ones that drop into the ureter and cause colic.

Colic pain moves with the stone, from loin to groin: flank first, then the inguinal region, then the scrotum or labia and front of the thigh (genitofemoral nerve, L1–L2). The X-rays and green arrows show stones stuck at the three narrowings. Pararenal pain: the kidney lies on the psoas major, a hip flexor, so extending the hip stretches the psoas and worsens pain from inflammation around the kidney.

Pus around the kidney stays inside the renal fascia. At the hilum the fascia is fixed to the renal vessels and ureter, so pus does not cross to the other kidney. Below, the front and back layers are only loosely joined, so pus can track down into the pelvis. Causes: an ascending urinary tract infection, spread through the blood (often Staph aureus), diabetes, and stones or cysts that block urine flow.

Find both suprarenal glands on top of the kidneys. The right one lies posterior to the IVC. The left one lies beside the aorta, next to the celiac trunk and its ganglion. Between the two glands, from right to left: IVC, right crus, celiac ganglion, celiac trunk, SMA (superior mesenteric artery), left crus.

Why it matters: the thin septum gives the gland its own compartment, firmly attached to the diaphragm. So when a loose kidney drops (nephroptosis), the gland stays put. A donor kidney can also be removed without damaging the gland.

Follow the layers from the kidney outward: fibrous capsule → perirenal fat → renal (Gerota's) fascia → pararenal fat. The suprarenal gland sits above the kidney, inside the same fascia, just under the diaphragm. The fascia's two layers are open at the bottom, which is why pus can track down.

Right gland: lies anterolateral to the right crus; the IVC lies anteromedial to it and the liver anterolateral. Left gland: lies medial to the upper half of the left kidney, posterior to the stomach and pancreas, near the spleen.

Examples: glucocorticoid = cortisol; mineralocorticoid = aldosterone. Aldosterone makes the kidney keep Na⁺ and water, which is how the cortex holds up blood volume and blood pressure (BP). Veins and lymph leave at the hilum, but arteries and nerves enter all over the surface.

Three arteries, each from the nearest big artery: superior from the inferior phrenic (above), middle from the aorta near the SMA (beside), inferior from the renal (below). They split into 50–60 twigs over the whole surface. One vein, asymmetric: the right is short and enters the IVC directly; the left is longer and drains into the left renal vein.

Find the short right suprarenal vein running straight into the IVC (pulled aside here). Because it is so short, it is easy to tear when the right gland is removed. Note the arteries from three sources entering from above, medially and below.
Find the longer left suprarenal vein running down to the left renal vein. The pancreas and spleen lie anterior to this gland (here lifted up).

A sympathetic path normally has two neurons with a synapse in a ganglion. Here the presynaptic fibers, from the lateral horn (IML, intermediolateral cell column) of cord segments T10–L1, pass through the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral) and celiac (prevertebral) ganglia without synapsing. They end directly on the chromaffin cells, which act as the second neuron but release epinephrine into the blood.

Solid lines = presynaptic fibers; dashed = postsynaptic. Fibers for the medulla cells pass the celiac ganglion without synapsing. Fibers for the gland's blood vessels synapse in the celiac ganglion first (dashed). The drawing shows only roots T5–T8 of the greater splanchnic nerve; the main supply comes from segments T10–L1.

A tumor of the chromaffin cells. It releases bursts of epinephrine and norepinephrine, so symptoms come in episodes: high BP, headache, sweating and a pounding heart (palpitations). Lab clue: high metanephrines (catecholamine breakdown products) in plasma or urine.

(A) Bifid pelvis: the renal pelvis splits in two because the ureteric bud divided partly. (B) Bifid ureter: two ureters join before the bladder (one opening); duplicated ureter: two separate openings into the bladder (uncommon). (C) Retrocaval ureter: the right ureter passes posterior to the IVC and can be compressed. (D) Horseshoe kidney: lower poles fuse; it stays at L3–L5 because the IMA (inferior mesenteric artery) blocks its ascent. (E) Pelvic kidney: never ascended; fed by the aortic bifurcation or common iliac artery. Don't mistake it for a pelvic tumor.

In the drawing (cross-section through the left kidney), the kidney sits in the gutter lateral to psoas major and anterior to quadratus lumborum, wrapped in perirenal fat and renal fascia. On the CT the patient's right is on your left (liver side): both kidneys sit in the gutters beside the vertebral body, with the round aorta just in front of the vertebra and the IVC (inferior vena cava) to its right.

Branches leave in three directions. Front: unpaired arteries to the gut: celiac trunk (T12), SMA (superior mesenteric artery, L1), IMA (inferior mesenteric artery, L3). Sides: paired arteries to the urogenital and endocrine organs (suprarenal, renal at L1, gonadal at L2). Back-sides: paired arteries to the diaphragm and body wall.

Find the left renal vein: it crosses anterior to the aorta, just below the SMA, to reach the IVC. The SMA can squeeze it against the aorta (nutcracker syndrome). Because the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins drain into it, the back-up causes blood in the urine and a left varicocele (swollen veins around the left testis).

Correction: the lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior rami of L1–L4 (often with a twig from T12). L5 joins part of L4 as the lumbosacral trunk, which belongs to the sacral plexus. The plexus forms inside psoas major, so all 7 branches come out around that muscle: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh, femoral, obturator, lumbosacral trunk.

Roots are on the right, nerves on the left. L1: iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal. L1–L2: genitofemoral. L2–L3: lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh. L2–L4: femoral and obturator. The bottom labels give direction: every nerve heads lateral except the obturator, which leaves the medial border of psoas. Cremasteric reflex: stroking the upper inner thigh makes the cremaster lift the testis.

Where each nerve shows up around psoas major:
  • Lateral border: iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal (on quadratus lumborum); lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh (across iliacus to just medial to the ASIS, anterior superior iliac spine); femoral (in the groove between psoas and iliacus).
  • Anterior surface: genitofemoral, the only one that pierces psoas; it splits above the inguinal ligament.
  • Medial border: obturator and lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5), both heading down into the true pelvis.

The trunk lies in the groove between the vertebral bodies and the medial edge of psoas; the IVC covers the right trunk and the aorta overlaps the left. Its ganglia send postganglionic fibers back into the spinal nerves, to vessels and sweat glands of the wall and leg. Its lumbar splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic fibers that synapse in small ganglia of the plexuses around the aorta, then reach the pelvic organs.

Psoas abscess: an infection, classically TB (tuberculosis) of the lumbar spine, spreads into the psoas sheath. Pus runs down this tube, deep to the inguinal ligament, and bulges in the upper thigh; lumbar plexus nerves in the muscle can be irritated. Psoas sign: the patient lies on the healthy side and the examiner extends the thigh. This stretches psoas, so an inflamed organ lying on it (right side: appendix) hurts.

An AAA (abdominal aortic aneurysm) is a bulge where the aortic wall is weak; a large one is felt as a pulsing mass left of the midline. The severe abdomen or back pain and the ~90% death rate belong to a rupture that is not recognized. The L4 point is the normal aorta: in thin people it can be pressed against the L4 body at the umbilicus to slow bleeding in the pelvis or legs.

The boxed labels on this and the next bone slides are the landmarks to know for that bone. The ASIS anchors the lateral end of the inguinal ligament. The PSIS (posterior superior iliac spine) lies under the skin dimples of the low back. The greater sciatic notch becomes the greater sciatic foramen once the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments close it.

The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) is the main sensory nerve of the perineum. It hooks around the ischial spine where the sacrospinous ligament attaches, so a finger in the vagina feels the spine and the needle goes just there. This numbs most of the perineum in childbirth. The front of the perineum is supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve (L1), which needs its own block (top label).

The linea terminalis is the ridge on the inner hip bone: arcuate line (ilium) + pecten pubis + pubic crest. With the sacral promontory and sacral ala it forms the pelvic brim, which divides the false pelvis above from the true pelvis below.

R marks the patient's right (on your left). Sacrum: midline wedge below L5, meeting each ilium at the sacroiliac joint lines. Ala: the wide wing; iliac crest: its top edge. ASIS: the bump on the wing's outer edge below the crest; AIIS (anterior inferior iliac spine): lower, above the hip joint. Obturator foramen: dark oval low on each side; its upper rim is the superior pubic ramus, its lower rim the ischiopubic ramus. Ischium: bone below and lateral to the foramen. Pubic symphysis: midline gap between the pubic bones.

A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint: bones held by ligament, here the strong interosseous sacroiliac ligament, so the sacroiliac joint barely moves. A secondary cartilaginous joint joins bones with a fibrocartilage pad (pubic symphysis, sacrococcygeal joint, IV = intervertebral disc joint). Zygapophysial joints are the small synovial facet joints between vertebral arches.

Don't confuse: sacrospinous runs from the sacrum to the ischial spine; sacrotuberous runs from the sacrum to the ischial tuberosity. Together they turn the sciatic notches into foramina: the greater sciatic foramen lies above the sacrospinous ligament, the lesser one between the two ligaments. They also keep the lower end of the sacrum from swinging up and back when body weight pushes its top down.

Left: the brim (edge of the inlet), part by part: sacral promontory (orange), margin of the sacral ala (green), then the linea terminalis = arcuate line (red) + pecten pubis (blue) + pubic crest (purple), meeting at the top of the pubic symphysis. Right, seen from below: the outlet (green) is diamond-shaped, with the pubic arch in front, the ischial tuberosities at the sides, and the sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx behind.

The pelvic brim (arrows) is the dividing line. Above it, the false (greater) pelvis (pink) is really the lowest part of the abdomen, between the iliac wings. Below it, the true (lesser) pelvis (blue) reaches down to the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani). Under the pelvic diaphragm lies the perineum (orange).

Hand test for the subpubic angle (the angle under the pubic symphysis): a male angle (pink) fits between the spread index and middle fingers; a female angle (green) fits between the spread thumb and index finger. The wider female angle and outlet make room for the baby's head.
The ischial spines sit closer together in males, which is a main reason the male outlet is smaller. Most female features (oval inlet, wide pubic arch, large outlet) make the birth canal wider.

What uses each exit:
  • Under the inguinal ligament: iliopsoas, femoral nerve, artery and vein → front of thigh.
  • Obturator canal (the obturator groove, closed below by the obturator membrane): obturator nerve and vessels → medial thigh.
  • Greater sciatic foramen: piriformis, sciatic nerve, gluteal vessels and nerves, pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels → buttock.
  • Lesser sciatic foramen: the pudendal nerve and vessels come back in → perineum; the obturator internus tendon goes out.

The pelvis is a ring, so it usually breaks in two places. A front-to-back crush (car crash) snaps the pubic rami and can tear the bladder or urethra behind them. A fall onto the feet can drive the femoral head through the acetabulum into the pelvis, injuring the organs, vessels and nerves there.

The plexus lies on the piriformis muscle on the back-side wall of the true pelvis, posterior to the internal iliac vessels. L4 and L5 reach it as the lumbosacral trunk, and most branches leave through the greater sciatic foramen. Its position next to the rectum and in the path of the fetal head is why rectal cancer and childbirth can injure it (leg pain).

Roots run down the middle. Left column = posterior divisions: superior gluteal (L4–S1), inferior gluteal (L5–S2), and the common fibular part of the sciatic. Right column = anterior divisions: the tibial part of the sciatic. Between them: posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh (S2–S3) and pudendal (S2–S4). The fibular and tibial parts travel together as the sciatic nerve (L4–S3).

Medial view of the pelvic side wall. Find the thick lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) crossing down to join S1. The superior gluteal artery passes between the lumbosacral trunk and S1; the inferior gluteal artery passes between S2 and S3. The thin pelvic splanchnic nerves leave S2–S4 and run toward the rectum.

Path: lumbar splanchnic nerves → superior hypogastric plexus (in front of L5, below the aortic split) → right and left hypogastric nerves → inferior hypogastric plexus beside the rectum, where they mix with the parasympathetic pelvic splanchnics. Don't confuse: sacral splanchnic nerves (from the sacral sympathetic trunk) are sympathetic; pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) are parasympathetic. Memory aid: parasympathetic = erection, sympathetic = ejaculation ('point and shoot').

Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from S2–S4. They supply the gut from the left colic (splenic) flexure down, plus all pelvic organs; the vagus nerve covers the gut above that point. Their effects: contract the rectum and bladder walls to empty them, and cause erection.

Stick diagram: aorta → common iliacs (at L4) → internal iliac (into the pelvis) and external iliac (becomes the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament). Just above the ligament the external iliac gives the inferior epigastric (which gives the cremasteric) and the deep circumflex iliac. @ = anastomosis with branches of the internal thoracic artery: inferior with superior epigastric, deep circumflex iliac with musculophrenic. These links can bypass a blocked aorta.

Unlabeled overview of the same arteries. Follow the aorta down: renal arteries to the sides, small paired lumbar arteries to the wall, the IMA leaving its front a little above the split, the split into common iliacs at L4, and the thin median sacral down the midline. Each common iliac splits into the internal iliac (dives into the pelvis) and the external iliac (runs along psoas). Near the inguinal ligament find the inferior epigastric going up and the deep circumflex iliac going out along the iliac crest.

The posterior division feeds the wall and buttock, not the organs. Iliolumbar: up to iliacus, psoas and quadratus lumborum. Lateral sacrals: into the anterior sacral foramina. Superior gluteal: its largest branch and usual end; it passes between the lumbosacral trunk and S1, then leaves through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis.

Don't confuse: the superior gluteal is the usual end of the posterior division. The inferior gluteal is normally the larger end branch of the anterior division (next slide) and leaves the pelvis below piriformis; only in some people does it come off the posterior division.

Colors: red arrows with black labels = both sexes; blue = male only; green = female only. @ = anastomosis: testicular artery with the artery to the ductus deferens; ovarian with uterine and vaginal; superior rectal (from the IMA) with middle and inferior rectal. The anterior division gives the organ branches and the obturator, then ends as the inferior gluteal (to the buttock) and the internal pudendal (to the perineum: inferior rectal, perineal, then dorsal and deep arteries of the penis or clitoris).

The obturator artery runs along the side wall to the obturator canal. In about 20% it arises from the inferior epigastric instead and descends past the femoral ring, so it can be cut during hernia repair. The superior vesical arteries come from the still-open start of the umbilical artery; the closed rest of it is the medial umbilical ligament.

Water (the ureter) passes under the bridge (the uterine artery) beside the cervix, near the lateral fornix of the vagina. When the uterine artery is clamped and tied during a hysterectomy, the ureter can be crushed, tied or cut with it. In males the bridge is the ductus deferens, which crosses over the ureter near the bladder.

Pelvic veins form plexuses around each organ. These connect with each other and drain mainly into the internal iliac vein. The rectal plexus is a portal–caval link: the superior rectal vein drains to the IMV (inferior mesenteric vein, portal system), while the middle and inferior rectal veins drain to the internal iliac vein (caval system). (m) = male only.

The pelvic plexuses connect, through the lateral sacral veins, with the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus), whose veins have no valves. Coughing or straining can push pelvic blood, and cancer cells, backward into it. That is how prostate cancer reaches the lumbar vertebrae and even the brain, skipping the lungs.
